title: Fossanova (1274)
hook: he dies on the way to a council, aged about forty-nine

segments.voice: Yesterday, straw: Thomas set down his pen, and tradition says everything he'd written seemed like straw next to what he'd seen. Your line was like straw. Did you set your work down, even for five minutes? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

A letter arrives from the pope, the early accounts say. There's to be a great council of the Church in Lyon, in France, and Thomas is wanted there. So the man who has stopped writing gets on the road anyway, heading north from Naples with his companions. Somewhere along the way he falls ill. He can't go on. The door that finally opens to him isn't a Dominican house at all. It belongs to the monks of another order, white-robed Cistercians, in an abbey called Fossanova. Today: the place where the road ends.
screen: `A LETTER FROM THE POPE.` → `ILL ON THE ROAD.` → `A DOOR AT FOSSANOVA.`

segments.voice: Tradition tells the last days quietly. The monks of Fossanova take him in and care for him. He's a stranger in their house, a friar, not one of their own, and they nurse him anyway. Tradition says that, sick as he was, he spoke to them about the Song of Songs, the love poem in the middle of the Bible. The great arguer, at the end, talking about love. When he receives Communion for the last time, the early accounts give him words of deep faith in Christ present in the sacrament, the same faith as the Corpus Christi hymns tradition credits to him. And then he dies there, among Cistercians, far from Paris and the lecture halls. His great book is unfinished. Paul, near his own end, says in the Douay-Rheims: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Thomas didn't finish his Summa. Catholics would say he finished his course. After his death, the Church named him a saint, and later a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for the whole Church. And Catholics gave him a nickname that stuck: the Angelic Doctor. People explain it in different ways. Some point to his long and careful writing on the angels. Others point to his life, which his companions remembered as pure and gentle, almost unearthly in its calm. Both reasons are told. Neither is the whole of it. There's one more quiet detail. The friar who gave his life to teaching was cared for at the end by monks of a praying order. A teacher, held by people who pray.
screen: `TAKEN IN BY STRANGERS.` · `THE SONG OF SONGS AT THE END.` · `A COURSE FINISHED, A BOOK NOT.` · `WHY THE ANGELIC DOCTOR?` · then, large: `I HAVE FINISHED MY COURSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for scholars. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who studies or teaches. A professor, a teacher you had in school, a student up too late, someone writing a book nobody may read. Picture their desk, their tired eyes. If you pray, you can ask God to give them light, and rest when their work runs out. If you don't, hold them in mind with thanks for what they've handed on. The bell holds the time.
Fossanova. The Cistercian abbey where Thomas, on his way to a council, fell ill, was cared for by monks, and died. Today's word.
Your line: the angelic doctor. Today, thank one teacher, past or present, with a message or a quiet word to God. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Thomas Aquinas, the Angelic Doctor, with Mass and sometimes with prayers for students and teachers, and some Catholic schools and universities honor him as a patron.

what it means: a Dominican teacher, unable to go on, taken in and nursed by Cistercian monks of another order.
what a scholar hears: summoned to the council of Lyon, he died on the way, at Fossanova; the title Doctor Angelicus is explained both by his treatise on angels and by his remembered purity of life.
